Electronic direct democracy anyone? It's not a far-fetched system. Switzerland is already using it, kinda, but I'm taking more about a complete direct democracy system. Time to move on to a system that is more open and a better representation of a population's will.

Direct democracy has scaling issues. It can't govern effectively in a country as large as the US. Switzerland is pretty much the upper limit of where direct democracy is still effective at legislation. It also requires a relatively homogenous population, which the USA has never had, on account of being a colonial state, instead of an aboriginal one.

The scaling issue seems kinda daunting at first but resolves itself once you consider that, while anyone can put forward legislation of any kind, only the most popular ideas (either because of existing majority consensus or because of a great campaign to educate and gain such consensus) will actually make it into law. Not to mention that with our current communication tech, if internet and telephone access is considered a right, any problems in regards to communication of the information on legislation being voted on and the ability to cast that vote are rendered moot.

There could be a set time limit that each proposed law can sit to gather votes or maybe a 24-hour voting period at the end of a campaignvon said proposal. Either way, the likelihood that the proposal will only be made law will rest entirely with the efforts of those who want to see it made law.

The homogenous population comment is the real dirty issue though. People are afraid that their proposals might not make it into law if the majority of the population doesn't want it made law. Or maybe there's a feeling that minority rights might get trampled by the rule of the majority.

The former is just the human fear of the unknown but something that is already happening now. Blatant case in point would be TPP. Who in the population of their nations actually wanted it to be adopted without even a national discussion amongst all the people that it would affect?

The latter is flawed thinking that has be taught to us in our schools. As the nature of direct democracy is based upon self-rule (the ability to make our own choices/freedom), it can never be direct democracy itself that is flawed and can instead only be the laws that people choose (with their free will) to implement with it, that can be flawed. In a true and direct democracy, there are no minorities because there are no socially-oriented divisions. Every minority group in the USA will be voting upon issues of US and regional law - not Pakistani, African, Jamaican, Islamic, Judaic or Mormon laws (for example). As US citizens with equal access to US voting rights, there are no minority groups and all are united as one. No one will no have to choose from only a left/right perspective (which benefits parties more than it does even their own voters).

This is exactly how true democracy can unify societies - these minorities ARE the majority but, only when there is no self-imposed or centrally imposed divisive spectrum and partisan centralisation. (Basically, if they can all agree on the same thing, then they are in the majority)

There is a UK political party (the People's Administration party) that has spent a lot of time on figuring it how to argue for and implement such a system and their website is where I am getting most of my talking points.

It's important to note that the American legal system doesn't need to be thrown out for Direct Democracy to do its work. We don't need a war or some great upheaval, we just need to enshrine the right for any eligible voter to cast a vote on any piece of legislation instead of limiting it to the right to voting for a "representative" to cast that vote for that eligible voter (and thousands of others in their riding). Then, existing legal system can slowly be changed, piece by piece, as the population sees fit but first there needs to be the willingness to work out and implement a secure voting system that can be accessed by all with internet it telephone access.
